c.tagline: Réunion's Créole capital on the Barachois seafront, a French-Indian Ocean gateway to the Piton de la Fournaise volcano and the island's soaring cirques.

taxi.fareNote: Metered taxis are available but relatively pricey; confirm the fare for longer trips. No major ride-hailing apps operate on Réunion. The urban Citalis buses and island-wide Car Jaune coaches are the budget option, but most visitors rent a car to reach the volcano and cirques.

emergency.note: Réunion is a French department with full French emergency services: 112 is the EU-wide number, 17 is the police and 15 is the SAMU medical service.

avoid.reason: The Le Chaudron district on the eastern edge has a reputation for unrest and petty crime and is best avoided at night.
Car break-ins are the main issue — leave nothing visible in rentals, and the city centre gets very quiet after dark.

hood_desc: The palm-lined seafront promenade with its row of old colonial cannons, food trucks and weekend strollers facing the Indian Ocean; the city's social heart and the best place for a sunset walk, a run or a café stop.

The historic core along Rue de Paris and Avenue de la Victoire, lined with restored Créole mansions, the cathedral, the Léon Dierx fine-arts museum, the Natural History Museum and the main shops; the walkable base for first-timers.

A large, modern district holding the university campus of Le Moufia, big shopping centres, the Papang cable-car terminus and the Chaudron neighbourhood; busy, local and the closest quarter to Roland Garros airport.
A residential hillside just above the centre with hospitals, embassy-style villas and cooler air; leafy and calmer, with sweeping views back over the city and out to sea.
A quiet residential hillside reached by a winding cliff road west of the city, offering panoramic ocean views, cooler temperatures and a green, laid-back pace away from the downtown bustle.
lodging: Radisson Hotel Saint Denis, La Reunion

water.note: Tap water is safe in the main towns, though boil-water notices can follow cyclones.

transit.pay: Citalis urban buses and the Papang cable car take cash or a rechargeable card; a single Citalis ride is about €1.60. Car Jaune interurban coaches to the rest of the island are paid by cash or card, with fares by distance (roughly €2-8).
transit.hours: Citalis buses run roughly 5:00 AM to 8:00 PM with limited evening service; the Papang aerial cable car links Bois-de-Nèfles and Le Chaudron. Taxis or a rental car fill the late-night gaps.
transit.note: Saint-Denis has no metro or passenger rail (the old colonial railway closed in the 1970s). The urban Citalis bus network covers the city, the island-wide Car Jaune coaches connect to other towns, and the Papang aerial cable car (opened 2022) serves the eastern heights; most visitors still rent a car to reach the volcano and cirques.

car.idp: Not required for EU licenses; an IDP is recommended for other nationalities

transit.m: Car Jaune 'Zéclair' express bus to Saint-Denis centre (~20-30 min)
Taxi to the city centre (15-20 min)

tip.r: Service is included by law ('service compris'); tipping is not expected, though rounding up or leaving a few euros for good service is appreciated.

food.name: Samoussas
food.desc: Crisp little triangles fried to order and filled with tuna, chicken, cheese or vegetables. The default Reunionese aperitif snack, sold everywhere.

landmarks: Le Barachois
Saint-Denis' breezy oceanfront esplanade, where cannons face the Indian Ocean surf and locals gather at sunset beneath swaying palms.
Rue de Paris
An elegant avenue of lambrequin-trimmed Creole mansions and gardens, the finest architectural promenade in Réunion's capital, leading from cathedral to Jardin de l'État.
Jardin de l'État
A stately 18th-century botanical garden of exotic trees and fountains, crowned by the colonnaded natural history museum at its head.
Cathédrale de Saint-Denis
The island's neoclassical cathedral of 1832, its palm-fringed facade and bell tower anchoring the historic heart of Réunion's capital.
Mosquée Noor-e-Islam
Opened in 1905 as the first mosque in France and its territories, its white-and-green minaret rises gracefully above the shops of Rue Maréchal Leclerc.
Musée Léon Dierx
Réunion's premier art museum in a former bishop's palace, surprising visitors with Gauguin, Picasso and a strong modern collection assembled by Ambroise Vollard.
Le Grand Marché
The capital's covered market overflowing with Malagasy wood carvings, vanilla, spices and woven baskets, the classic stop for Creole souvenirs.
Notre-Dame de la Délivrance
A twin-towered 19th-century church rising photogenically above the Rivière Saint-Denis, built in thanksgiving for deliverance from a cholera epidemic.
Préfecture de Saint-Denis
The dignified former French East India Company headquarters of the 1730s, one of the island's oldest buildings, fronting manicured waterfront gardens.
Musée d'Histoire Naturelle
A 19th-century natural history museum near the Barachois with mounted birds, whale skeletons, and displays on Réunion's volcanic origins and endemic wildlife.

train.note: Reunion has had no railway since the Chemin de Fer de La Reunion, which ran along the coast from Saint-Benoit through Saint-Denis to Saint-Pierre, closed in 1976; parts of its cliff-side alignment were absorbed into the coast road. A tram-train scheme for the north coast was cancelled, and although new guided-transport projects are discussed periodically, nothing is operating. There is no international rail, as Reunion is an island.

bus.note: No coach crosses a border from an island in the middle of the Indian Ocean. The island-wide Car Jaune network (https://www.carjaune.re/) radiates from the gare routiere in central Saint-Denis, with express lines running down the west coast to Saint-Pierre in about 1 hr 45 min, east to Saint-Benoit, and a direct link to Roland Garros airport a few kilometres east of the city. Urban and near-suburban services around Saint-Denis are run by Citalis (https://www.citalis.re/), which has introduced free travel on its city network. Tickets are bought from the driver or loaded onto a rechargeable card, and services are much reduced on Sundays and public holidays.

intl.to: Port Louis (Mauritius) - sails from Port Reunion at Le Port, about 20 km west of Saint-Denis

ferry.note: Reunion's only passenger sea link is the Mauritius Trochetia between Port Reunion at Le Port - 20-30 minutes from Saint-Denis by road or Car Jaune - and Port Louis in Mauritius, an overnight crossing of roughly 11 hours. It sails a few times a month rather than daily, is frequently disrupted during the January-to-March cyclone season, and cabins and any vehicle space must be reserved well ahead through the operator or its Reunion agent. Saint-Denis itself has no working harbour, and there is no passenger service to Madagascar, Mayotte or mainland Africa.

half.name: La Roche Écrite
half.blurb: A 2,276-metre summit above Saint-Denis reached through cloud forest, its lookout delivering staggering views into the cirques of Mafate and Salazie.
